notes.meaning: Paul is writing from prison. He says he is Christ's prisoner, held because he preached that the good news is for Gentiles (people who are not Jewish) too. He starts a prayer here, then breaks off and picks it up again in verse 14.
Paul is not doubting that they have heard. He is gently reminding them. God gave him a 'stewardship,' a job of handing out God's grace (his free, undeserved kindness), especially to the Gentiles.
Paul did not invent this message or learn it from others. God showed it to him directly. A 'mystery' here means a secret God kept until now. Paul has already touched on it earlier in this letter.

As they read his letter, they will see how well Paul understands this secret. The 'mystery of Christ' is God's plan to welcome Gentiles through Christ on the same terms as Jews. Reading the Bible carefully, and taking it to heart, is how we come to understand it.

The Old Testament prophets did say Gentiles would come to God. But they did not see it as clearly as it is shown now. They did not know Gentiles would come in without keeping the law of Moses. The Holy Spirit has now made this plain to the apostles and to the prophets of the New Testament church.

Here is the secret spelled out. Gentiles who believe share the same inheritance as believing Jews. They belong to the same body, the church, with Christ as its head. And they share the same promises, including the promise of the Holy Spirit. All this comes through being joined to Christ and through the gospel.

Paul did not make himself a minister. God made him one as a free gift, not because he earned it. God's power worked in him, turning a man who once fought the gospel into its servant. What God calls people to do, he also equips them to do.

Paul calls himself 'less than the least' of all God's people. He even makes up a new word to say it. He never forgot that he once hurt the church. Yet he speaks of Christ's riches as 'unsearchable,' like a mine too deep ever to reach the bottom.

Paul's job was to shine a light so everyone could see God's plan. This plan was hidden in God's mind for ages. God made everything, so he has every right to keep his plans hidden until the right time. The God who made all things is also able to save Jews and Gentiles alike.

God wants to show his wisdom through the church. Even the angels in heaven watch and learn from it. God's wisdom is 'manifold,' meaning many-sided, like many colors. The church, made of Jews and Gentiles together, is like a stage or a mirror where that wisdom is seen.
Bringing in the Gentiles was no afterthought. It was God's eternal plan from before time began. That plan has now been carried out in Jesus Christ.

Because of Jesus, we can come to God freely. We can speak openly, like children talking to a loving father. This boldness comes through faith in Christ, our go-between with God. It is not pride, but trust that God will hear us.

Paul worries more that they will lose heart than about his own suffering. He tells them not to give up because he is in prison. His sufferings show how much God loves them, since God sent his apostles to suffer for them. That is why his troubles are their 'glory,' their honor.
Paul now returns to the prayer he began in verse 1. He kneels before the Father. Kneeling shows humble respect for God. Paul prays because teaching does no good unless God makes it fruitful.

God's people in heaven and on earth make up one family. They take their name from him, much as children carry their father's name. Jews and Gentiles now belong to the same household. Some older writers also count the angels as part of this one family.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read it as 'every family.' Every family group, of angels in heaven and people on earth, gets the name 'family' from God the Father.

notes.meaning: Paul's first request is for inner strength. He asks that God's Holy Spirit would make them strong in their soul. That strength helps them trust, resist temptation, and do what is right. God gives out of his endless riches, not in small amounts.

Paul prays that Christ would make his home in their hearts. Faith is like opening the door to let him in. Where his Spirit lives, Christ lives. Paul also wants their love to be deep, like a tree with strong roots or a house on a firm foundation.

Paul prays they will be strong enough to grasp how great Christ's love is. He uses four measures to show how huge it is. Older writers explain it this way: wide enough to reach all people, long enough to last forever, deep enough to reach the worst sinner, and high enough to lift us to heaven. We grasp this together with all believers, not on our own.

Christ's love is bigger than we can ever fully understand. Yet we can know it truly and keep learning more of it. Paul's highest request is that they be 'filled with all the fullness of God.' This does not mean becoming God. It means being filled, as much as we can hold, with the grace God gives his people.

differ.view: Being filled with God's fullness means being filled with his love and holiness. That leaves no room for sin, so believers can be freed from sin in this life.

Whoever has Christ has all they need to be made complete in God. But no believer grows so far that they stop needing to grow. In this life, the highest goal is an earnest desire to keep making progress.

notes.meaning: Paul ends his prayer with praise. God can do far more than anything we ask or can even imagine. We have already seen his power at work in us. That gives us good reason to trust him for more.
All glory belongs to God. He is praised in the church and through Jesus Christ. That praise will go on through every generation, forever. 'Amen' means 'so be it,' and so it will be.
